notFound.title: Page not found
notFound.heading: This page isn't on the list
notFound.body: Like a resource blocked by a Content-Security-Policy, this address isn't allowed here, mostly because it doesn't exist.

learn.title: What is a CSP?
learn.description: Content-Security-Policy explained for people who don't write code: what it is, why it blocks marketing tools, and how to talk about it with your IT team.
learn.heading: What is a Content-Security-Policy?
learn.lead: It's a list your website gives to every visitor's browser, saying which places the page is allowed to use content from. Anything not on the list is refused.
learn.exampleLine1: **Line 1:** code (scripts) may only come from our own website and from Google Tag Manager.
learn.exampleLine2: **Line 2:** images may only come from our own website, or be embedded directly in the page.
learn.why1: A web page is assembled from many pieces: your own code, but also scripts from analytics, advertising, chat or testing tools. If an attacker manages to slip their own script into a page, for example through a vulnerable plugin or a compromised supplier, that script can read what visitors type, including passwords and card numbers. Attacks like this have hit well-known retailers and airlines.
learn.why2: The policy is a safety net: even if malicious code gets in, the browser refuses to run it or to send data to places that aren't on the list. For sites that take payments, standards such as PCI DSS now expect this kind of control.
learn.tools1: From the browser's point of view, a new analytics tag or A/B testing tool is just more code coming from a new place. If that place isn't on the list, it's blocked, exactly like an attack would be. The browser can't tell a tool you chose from a malicious one: only the list can.
learn.tools2: So adding a tool usually means adding its addresses to the list. Most vendors publish exactly what to add. Some also ask for permissions that loosen the protection for everyone, like allowing code written directly in the page (`'unsafe-inline'`). That's where your security team may push back, and that's a reasonable conversation, not a refusal.

directive.definition: One rule of the policy, for one kind of content: `script-src` for code, `img-src` for images, and so on.

source.definition: An allowed place in a rule: a website address, or a keyword like `'self'` (your own site).

unsafeInline.definition: Allows code written directly inside the page. Many marketing tools need it; it also weakens the protection the most.

nonce.definition: A secret one-time code the site puts on the scripts it trusts. It's the modern, safer alternative to `'unsafe-inline'`, and most tag managers support it.

reportOnly.definition: A trial mode: the browser reports what it would block, but blocks nothing. Teams use it to test a policy safely. To receive those reports, [see what your policy blocks](/reporting).

learn.askTitle: How to ask for a change
learn.ask2: [Paste it into the analyzer](/) and pick the tools you want to use.
learn.ask3: Copy the message it writes for your IT or security team. It lists exactly what to add, why, and the risks to weigh.
learn.none: Many sites don't send one. [Build a policy](/build): start from a blank policy, add the tools your site should allow, and every line says who asked for it.

about.title: About
about.description: An independent, free tool to understand Content-Security-Policies. Your policy never leaves your browser.
about.lead: A free, independent tool to help everyone who works on a website, not only developers, understand its Content-Security-Policy and talk about it with confidence.
about.privacyTitle: Your policy stays in your browser
about.privacy: Everything is computed on your device. The policy you paste is never sent to a server. Share links keep the policy after the `#` of the address, a part browsers never send to servers. The tools you describe yourself in the policy builder are also remembered in this browser, so you can pick them again: they stay on this device, anyone using the same browser can see them, and “Forget the tools saved in this browser” removes them. The analyzer keeps your last 10 analyses there too, with the tools you picked, to reopen one later: the same applies, and you can delete them or stop keeping a history under the list.
about.count: To know whether the site is useful, we count visits and a few actions: analysing a policy, trying the example, opening a share link, adding a tool, copying a report or the snippet, building a policy and copying it. For each one we keep a line with the time, what happened and the page, tool or report involved, for 13 months. No cookies, no third-party service, nothing that identifies you, and never your policy or your site address.
about.sourceSpec: Directive behaviour follows the [W3C Content Security Policy Level 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/) specification.
about.sourceEvaluator: Security findings come from Google's [CSP Evaluator](https://github.com/google/csp-evaluator) library (Apache-2.0), the same checks as csp-evaluator.withgoogle.com.
about.sourceVendors: What each tool needs comes from the vendor's official documentation, linked on every entry with the date it was last checked. No vendor pays to be listed or influences the results.
about.catalogue: Vendors change their requirements. If an entry is outdated or a tool is missing, [open an issue]({issues}) with a link to the official documentation.
about.own: We follow our own advice. This site sends two policies: a header for what only a header can do (refusing to be embedded in other sites), and a `<meta>` tag with strict rules where scripts and styles are allowed by their exact fingerprint (hash).

find.title: Find your website's CSP
find.description: Step-by-step ways to find the Content-Security-Policy of any website, for non-technical people and developers.
find.lead: Your website sends its policy along with every page, usually out of sight. Pick one of these ways to get a copy. The snippet is the quickest; the terminal is for developers. An error message doesn't contain the policy, but it tells you which rule blocked something.

console.title: Copy it with a snippet
console.intro: About a minute, in Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari. No technical knowledge needed.
console.step1: Open the page of your website you're interested in: the homepage, a product page, the checkout…
console.step2: Open the developer tools: [[F12]] on Windows, [[⌘]] [[⌥]] [[J]] on Mac. In Safari, first turn on *Settings › Advanced › Show features for web developers*.
console.step4: Copy this snippet, paste it into the console and press [[Enter]].
console.step5: The policy is now in your clipboard: [paste it into the analyzer](/).
console.note: The snippet only reads: it loads the page you're on again, keeps its policy and copies it. It sends nothing anywhere.
console.safeQuestion: Is it safe to paste code into the console?
console.safeAnswer: Be careful with code from people you don't know: anything pasted into the console runs as you, on that website. That's why Chrome and Firefox may ask you to type `allow pasting` first. Every line of this snippet is shown above, so you can check what it does before running it.
console.syncQuestion: I see a yellow warning about "synchronous XMLHttpRequest"
console.syncAnswer: It's harmless. The snippet reads the page in one go, without waiting, because that's the only way the browser lets it copy the result for you.
console.refusedQuestion: I see an error such as "Refused to connect"
console.refusedAnswer: Your policy blocks the snippet itself. Use the Network tab instead.

devtools.title: Look in the Network tab
devtools.intro: No code involved: you read the policy in the browser's developer tools.

chrome.label: Chrome & Edge
steps: Reload the page: [[F5]], or [[⌘]] [[R]] on Mac.
Click the first line of the list. It has your page's address and the type *document*.
Find `content-security-policy`, right-click its value and choose *Copy value*.

safari.label: Safari
steps: Turn on *Settings › Advanced › Show features for web developers*.
Reload the page and click the first resource.
In **Headers**, find `Content-Security-Policy` under *Response* and copy its value.

devtools.note: No `content-security-policy` line? Look for `content-security-policy-report-only`, or search the page source: the policy may be inside the page.

source.title: Search the page source
source.intro: Some sites write their policy inside the page instead of sending it separately.
steps: Right-click the page and choose *View Page Source*.
Copy the whole `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" …>` tag. The analyzer reads it as is.

terminal.title: From a terminal
terminal.intro: Shows the headers your server returns. Paste the whole output into the analyzer.
terminal.caption: Run in a terminal, with your site's address
terminal.whereQuestion: Where is the policy usually configured?
where: **CDN or edge:** CloudFront response headers policies, Cloudflare Transform Rules, Fastly, Akamai.
**Framework:** helmet (Express), Next.js `headers()`, Django CSP, Spring Security, Rails `content_security_policy`.
**HTML template or CMS plugin** for `<meta>` policies.

errors.title: Read an error message
errors.intro: An error message isn't your policy, so there's nothing to copy here. But it tells you what was blocked and why. When a tool doesn't work, the console ([[F12]], **Console** tab) often shows a red message like this:
errors.blocked: The address after *Refused to load*: a script from `cdn.vendor.example`.
errors.allows: The values after the rule name.
errors.note: Don't paste the message into the analyzer: it only shows one rule of your policy. To check the whole policy, get a copy with the [snippet](#console) or one of the other ways.

items.definition: The checkout, the login page or a blog on another platform often have their own. Check the page where your tool must run.

items.term: There can be more than one
items.definition: Several headers, or a header and a `<meta>` tag. Something must be allowed by all of them, so paste them together.
`Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` only reports problems, often while a team tests a new policy.

items.term: It may come from somewhere unexpected
items.definition: A CDN, a firewall or a security plugin can add or change the header. Ask your developers where it's configured.

reporting.title: CSP violation reports
reporting.description: Get a report each time your Content-Security-Policy blocks something: the two headers to add, what a report looks like, and how to read it.
reporting.heading: See what your policy blocks
reporting.lead: Browsers can send you a short report each time your policy blocks something, from every visitor's browser. It's how you find what a new policy breaks before your visitors tell you, and how you see attacks being stopped.

setup.title: Set it up
setup.intro: Two headers: one names the address that receives the reports, the other tells the policy to use it.
setup.caption: Response headers, sent with every page

parts.definition: Gives an address a name, here `csp`. It must use https: browsers ignore any other address.
Sends this policy's reports to the address named `csp`. Chrome and Edge, Firefox (since version 149) and Safari (since 16.4) support it.
The older way, with the address written in the policy. Browsers that understand `report-to` ignore it, so it only matters for older browsers. Keeping both costs nothing.

setup.meta: Reporting only works in headers: a policy written in a `<meta>` tag can't send reports.
setup.reportOnly: Trying out a new policy? Send it as `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` with the same reporting lines. Nothing is blocked, and you get a report for everything that would be. When the reports stop, switch to `Content-Security-Policy`.

format.title: What a report looks like
format.intro: The browser sends it to your address as a `POST` request with a small JSON document. Your server doesn't need to answer anything: the browser ignores the reply.
format.label: Report format

current.intro: Sent with `Content-Type: application/reports+json`. Each report has a `type` and a `body`:

legacy.intro: Sent with `Content-Type: application/csp-report`, one report per request:
legacy.names: The same facts with older names: `document-uri` is the page, `blocked-uri` what was blocked, `effective-directive` the line that applied. A blocked address from another site is shortened to its origin (scheme, host and port).

type.definition: `csp-violation` for policy reports. The same address can receive other kinds of browser reports, so check it first.

page.definition: The page where it happened, also in `url`. `referrer` is the page the visitor came from.

blocked.definition: What was blocked: an address, or `inline` for code written in the page, or `eval` for code built from text.

directive.definition: The kind of resource, as the line of the policy that applied: `script-src-elem` is a `<script>` tag, `img-src` an image. The analyzer explains each one.

disposition.definition: `enforce` when the browser blocked it. Reports from a `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` policy carry another value: nothing was blocked.

where.definition: Where the code that triggered it is, when the browser knows.

sample.definition: The first 40 characters of the blocked inline code. Only sent when the line has `'report-sample'`.

policy.definition: The whole policy the page was sent. Useful when pages have different ones.

context.definition: How long ago it happened, in milliseconds, and which browser sent it.

items.term: An address of a tool you use
items.definition: The policy is missing it. Add it to the line named in `effectiveDirective`, or let [Will my tools work?](/) find what the tool needs.
Code written in the page. Give your own `<script>` and `<style>` blocks a nonce or a hash: the [builder](/build) and the analyzer compute hashes.
Code built from text, usually by a library or a tool. It needs `'unsafe-eval'`, or a newer version of the library that doesn't.
Often browser extensions, or software on the visitor's device adding code to every page. Group them and look for patterns before changing the policy.
Something new in the pages, or a tool that changed what it loads. Compare with what was published that day.
The address is public, so treat reports as untrusted data: never show their content as HTML, and limit how many you accept.
Page addresses with their query strings, the previous page, code samples. Keep them like logs: only what you need, not for long.
One broken line on a busy page sends a report from every visit. Count them by blocked address and directive rather than reading them one by one.
A small endpoint of your own is enough to start. Error tracking services and dedicated report collectors also accept these formats.

trustedTypes.title: Trusted Types
trustedTypes.description: What Trusted Types change in a page, the two Content-Security-Policy lines that turn them on, how to roll them out safely, and what to check for third-party tools.
trustedTypes.heading: Trusted Types: only checked code goes into the page
trustedTypes.lead: A common way in for malicious code is a page's own JavaScript writing text it received, from a link, a form or a server, into the page as HTML or code. With Trusted Types on, the browser refuses plain text in those places: only values that went through a check your site defined are accepted.

changes.title: What changes in the page
changes.intro: These ways of turning text into page content or code stop accepting plain text:

sinks.definition: `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write`, an iframe's `srcdoc`, and parsing HTML with `DOMParser`.
`eval`, `new Function`, and `setTimeout` or `setInterval` given a string.
A `<script>` element's `src` or text, and the address of a worker.

changes.error: The browser blocks the call and throws an error, so the rest of that code doesn't run either. Chrome's console shows two messages: the policy's, then the error the code receives.

parts.definition: Turns Trusted Types on. `'script'` is the only value.

The names of the policies scripts may create, here `sanitize`. Creating one with another name fails. Without this line, any name is allowed; `'none'` allows none, and `'allow-duplicates'` lets two policies share a name, which weakens the list.

policies.title: Policies: the checks your code goes through
policies.intro: A policy is a small named function your site writes once. Code that needs to write HTML asks the policy, which returns a value the browser accepts:
policies.caption: JavaScript, in your own code
policies.explain: The check itself is up to you: here a sanitizer library such as DOMPurify removes anything that could run. Most of the time the better fix is not to write HTML at all: `textContent` puts text in the page without a policy.
policies.default: A policy named `default` is applied automatically to every plain text that reaches those places. It helps while moving old code over, but it hides where the risky calls are: keep it temporary, and as strict as you can.

rollout.title: Rolling it out
rollout.reports: Set up [violation reports](/reporting), so you see what the browser would refuse, on every page and in every visitor's browser.
rollout.trial: Turn Trusted Types on in a **report-only** policy. Nothing breaks: every call that would be refused sends a report, with `trusted-types-sink` as what was blocked and a sample naming the call, such as `Element innerHTML`, followed by the start of the text.
rollout.trialCaption: Response header, added beside your current policy
rollout.fix: Fix each place the reports name:
fixes: Use `textContent` instead of `innerHTML` where the content is plain text.
Pass HTML that must stay HTML through a named policy that sanitizes it.
Replace `eval` and string timers with real functions.
Keep a `default` policy only for code you can't change yet.
rollout.enforce: When the reports stop, move both lines into your `Content-Security-Policy`, with `trusted-types` listing the policy names your pages create.

tools.title: Third-party tools
tools.intro: Tag managers, analytics, chat widgets and consent banners write HTML and load scripts. Under Trusted Types, a tool that doesn't create its own policy is refused, or goes through your `default` policy if you have one. A tool that does create one needs its name listed in `trusted-types`.
tools.catalogue: None of the [tools in our catalogue](/vendors) say in their official documentation whether they work with Trusted Types, or which policy names they use. Test each one in report-only mode first, and ask the vendor: when one documents it, the catalogue will say so.

items.definition: Chrome and Edge since version 83, Firefox since 148, Safari since 26. Older browsers ignore both lines: nothing breaks, and nothing is protected there.
Trusted Types only work on https pages (and on `localhost` while developing).
Trusted Types stop text being turned into code inside the page. Keep a strict `script-src` too: it decides which scripts load at all.
